newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China dissident's HK visit stirs controversy.
newsitem.headline: China dissident's HK visit stirs controversy.

text.p: Chinese dissident and leader of the 1989 Tiananmen Square democracy movement Chai Ling has stirred controversy in Hong Kong by visiting the territory weeks before China takes it back from Britain.
The incident added a twist to a debate in Hong Kong over political liberties, which future leader Tung Chee-hwa plans to restrict after the territory returns to Chinese rule on July 1.

On Monday, the self-exiled Chai voiced concern about Hong Kong's future and urged the People's Liberation Army (PLA), whose second advance garrison party arrived in Hong Kong on the same day, not to repeat the army's crackdown on the 1989 democracy movement in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Chai, 28, who lives in the United States, arrived in Hong Kong last weekend on a one-week visa.
She said Hong Kong might set a democratic example to China in the future, and spoke in favour of political reform in her country, to which she hoped eventually to return.
China's mission in Hong Kong, the Xinhua News Agency branch, denounced Hong Kong authorities for allowing the territory to become a "base for subversion" against China.
The Hong Kong government has described Chai's visit as private and has said it will not allow the territory to be used by individuals or organisations with a violent political agenda.
Emily Lau, a pro-democracy legislator, dismissed China's reaction and said there was no question of subversion.
"I don't think allowing people like Chai Ling and others to come would be turning Hong Kong into a base of subversion. I think these Xinhua people should not be so paranoid," she said.

Pro-China newspapers Wen Wei Po and Ta Kung Pao attacked Chai's visit, while the independent Sing Tao daily said Hong Kong should allow more visits by pro-democracy activists because they would have a positive impact on the development of China.
Chai was a leader of the 1989 movement in Beijing that was crushed by PLA tanks with heavy loss of life, forcing her and other activists to flee into exile.
A pro-China politician accused Governor Chris Patten of mischief-making by allowing Chai into Hong Kong.
"The Chinese government has been politically embarrassed over the entry of a wanted criminal into the territory on the eve of return to China," said Lau Siu-kai.

"It seems to be more of a mischievous act by Chris Patten rather than a move to set standards for the post-handover government which will by no means allow the entry of criminals," Lau told the South China Morning Post newspaper.
Hong Kong has been split by future leader Tung's plan to ban foreign funding of political groups and to limit the right to protest, moves fiercely opposed by the pro-democracy camp.

In a new sign of strain, the territory's Chief Secretary Anson Chan, whom Tung is keeping on after the handover, said the future government must move quickly to install an internationally credible legislature after the flag change.
"We have an obligation to the community to ensure they are represented by a credible and authoritative legislature," Chan said at a conference in the Philippines on Monday.
Anxiety over the future of democracy is running high because of China's plan to replace the elected Hong Kong legislature on July 1 with an appointed body until new elections in 1998.
